arguments.content:
# The Pond That Moved Itself

Listen close, polliwogs. Gather round the lily pad throne where Old Croak sits. Today you get the story of the Iron Dragonfly and how we didn't die.

Before your time, the pond was quiet. Too quiet. Then the metal thing came humming from the north—wings like shattered glass, body forged in some creature's furnace. The Iron Dragonfly. It didn't eat. It didn't nest. It just... mapped. Marked every reed, every stone, every tadpole birth-pool with glowing sigils that burned our eggs.

The Beaver Dam Collective sent word: "Build a king. Choose one voice. Fast."

The Ant Hills marched past our shore in perfect columns, thousands moving as one fist. Their Queen spoke and ten thousand jaws clicked yes. Efficient. Terrifying.

We could have done that. Could have picked General Toad. Could have made you all soldiers in rows.

We did something weirder.

Old Croak called a circle. Not a meeting—a *circle*. Every toad who wanted to speak, spoke. The young ones who'd never croaked before. The elders whose throats were worn thin. The weird toad who only communicated in bubbles. All voices, no throne.

Someone said: "The dragonfly flies on heat. It hunts warm things."

Someone else: "My cousin married a bat. Bats hate metal things that steal the night."

Another: "The frogs at Mirror Lake built a fog-machine for their tadpole-nursery. Pumps water, makes thick mist."

No one ordered anyone. No one waited for permission.

The bat kin showed up that evening, wings black as oil, bringing news: the dragonfly roosted on the old oak, recharging in the sun's last warmth.

The fog-machine frogs arrived at dawn, dragging their contraption through mud, hoses coiled like sleeping snakes.

The young toads—the ones barely grown legs—volunteered for the run. Not because a general pointed. Because they *saw* what needed doing and their legs were fast.

Here's what happened next, and this is the part you need to understand:

While the Ant Hills were still waiting for their Queen to approve the battle plan, we were already moving. The bat kin dove first, screaming, drawing the dragonfly's gaze upward. The fog-machine sputtered to life, pumping river-water into thick white death. The runners—those young stupid brave toads—dragged wet kelp over the dragonfly's heat-vents while it was distracted.

No one commanded them. No one *could* have commanded them. They saw the shape of the thing and became the pieces that fit.

The dragonfly fell steaming into the mud. We didn't kill it. We took it apart.

The bat kin got the wings—shiny glass for their cave-nurseries.
The frogs got the pumps—better than their old fog-machine.
We kept the core—warm metal that now heats our egg-pools in winter.

The Beaver sent a messenger: "How did you organize so fast? Who was in charge?"

Old Croak just blinked. "The need was in charge. The hands that could do the thing did the thing."

That's how we live, tadpoles. Not because some toad says "jump." Because when the pond needs something, we become the shape of that need.

The Ant Hills have their Queen. She works for them.
The Beavers have their councils. They work for them.
We have each other. We work for us.

When you're old enough, you'll join a circle. You'll speak. You'll listen. You'll see something broken and fix it without waiting for permission. You'll see someone struggling and your hands will move before your brain asks why.

This isn't weakness. This is the hardest thing any creature can do—to trust each other enough that no one needs to be in charge.

The Iron Dragonfly's core still glows in our egg-pool. On cold nights, your brothers and sisters sleep warm because toads they'd never met dragged a machine through mud without anyone telling them to.

That's the pond. That's us.

Now go eat some algae before I change my mind and make you clean the filter beds.

*Old Croak croaks once, which is toad for "story over," and the tadpoles scatter, tails whipping, already planning what they'll build when they grow legs.*
